chunks.text: The tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is the sole species in its genus, a legume in the family Fabaceae, and is indigenous to the dry savannas of tropical Africa, particularly the Sudanian belt from Sudan's Kordofan region west across the Sahel. Long cultivated in Asia, it has since naturalised across the tropics and subtropics, and Spanish and Portuguese colonists carried it to Mexico and Central America in the 16th century. It is a long-lived, slow-growing tree reaching 25-30 metres with an irregular, vase-shaped crown up to 12 metres wide and a trunk that can measure 7.5 metres in circumference; its heartwood is hard and dark red while the sapwood is softer and yellowish. The evergreen, feathery leaves are paripinnately compound, and the red-and-yellow flowers give way to hard-shelled, indehiscent brown pods 12-15 cm long containing 1-12 seeds embedded in sour-sweet pulp; a mature tree can yield up to 225 kg of pods a year. The name comes from Arabic 'tamr hindi,' meaning 'Indian date.'

chunks.source: Wikipedia — Tamarind (culinary, medicinal and other uses)
chunks.text: Tamarind pulp is used across many cuisines: in Indian cooking for chutneys, sambhar and curries; in Philippine sinigang and Indonesian sayur asem as a souring agent; and in Western products such as Worcestershire sauce and HP Sauce. Seeds yield pectin used to stabilise jellies and jams. In traditional medicine it has been used as a laxative, as a fever poultice in Southeast Asia, for skin irritation, and in various regional folk remedies for ailments ranging from leprosy to parasitic worms, though these are traditional rather than clinically established uses. The heartwood is durable and insect-resistant, if hard to work, and is used for furniture, boats, carvings, mortars and pestles, and traditional kris daggers; the pulp is also traditionally used in some Buddhist countries to polish brass, copper and bronze. Tamarind fruit and leaves make up roughly half the diet of ring-tailed lemurs in Madagascar when available, but the fruit is toxic to dogs. India and the United States are today's leading commercial producers, with a gap-free tamarind genome sequenced in 2025 showing about 30,753 protein-coding genes.
